The *Complete Collection of the Venerable Zibo* has already been circulated throughout the monastic communities (*conglin*).

In addition, there are the four fascicles of the *Collected Excerpts* compiled by Qian Qizhong and the four fascicles of the *Essential Teachings of the Heart* by Lu Fu. Master Anzhi brought a copy from the collection of the Zhou family of Wujiang.
This was composed by the Venerable Master during his middle years. His lay disciples, Miao Zhongchun, Zhou Jihua, and Zhou Zijie, attended upon him at his side and transcribed it by hand.
I have collated various editions of this work, selecting those passages not included in his collected works, and arranged them into four volumes titled the *Separate Collection of Zibo*.
I have appended this preface to its end, noting that within the five houses of the Chan school...
As for the transmission of the lamp: since the Southern Song dynasty’s relocation to the south, the lineage flourished greatly from Shimen Miaoxi through to Gaofeng Duanya and Zhongfeng.
From the Yuan dynasty until the early Ming, it reached a second peak of prosperity with Yuansou Jizhao, Xiaoyin, Zhushi, Puban, and Jitan.
For two hundred years thereafter, the transmission of the lamp had become silent and desolate. Then the Venerable One emerged in Eastern Wu, his spirit...
The Emperor is like a sovereign who treads upon the world; when karmic conditions manifest as disturbances, they surge forth from the earth.
This truly concerns the rise and fall of the national destiny and the flourishing or decline of the Dharma. One must not recklessly attempt to measure this with an ordinary mind or worldly wisdom.

When the Venerable One appeared in the world during the Wanli era, it was precisely the time when the nation was at its zenith, enjoying peace and prosperity. Yet, the foreign tribes in their sable temples and felt robes were sowing seeds of calamity.
The Master, through the power of his compassionate vows and precepts, resided in the city of Rājagṛha and preached the Dharma.

He spread the compassionate clouds of the Holy Mother and opened the sun of wisdom for the Sage Sovereign. It was hoped that the mining taxes might be abolished, the prohibitions against political factions removed, the military frontiers cleared, and the current of slaughter turned back.
Yet the petty crowd set their nets to ensnare those of like mind and used the "Satanic Book" as a weapon to strike one another down. The Master—
Thereupon, having cast aside this illusory body and brought to rest the calamities of the pure stream, the banner of the Dharma has fallen and state policy has daily deviated from the truth.
The reins of imperial authority have shifted downward, and the Emperor’s resolve has been unraveled. Demonic forces invade from without, and neither humans nor devas provide protection.

Examining the records of the origins and end of the "Specter Book" (Yao-shu), one knows the causes for the destruction and erosion of the karmic age; though these are bound by the causes of past karma, they are indeed a phenomenon that has occurred since antiquity.
We have not yet seen such a one. Since ancient times, it has always been said that great ministers who transform the age must be those descended from divine spirits;

how much more so for the Dharma King and Guide—could he possibly not appear at rare intervals? This Venerable One possesses the adamantine mind and is endowed with the power of Nārāyaṇa; he could raise his hand and strike Mount Sumeru.
A single exhalation can swallow the vast ocean; when the golden-winged Garuda beats its wings, the dragon princes follow as his prey—how much more so the fish and eels?
When the lion roars, even the fragrant elephant loses its excrement in terror—how much more so the jackal?
Now that the man has passed away, the lamp of the Dharma is extinguished. The fish and eels dance about while the jackal howls. It is the same.
At that time, the Great Virtuous One abandoned the saffron robe for the black one and returned to the human realm, resolving the great matter through his dream-like travels.

It was as if an aged general, having withdrawn his entire army to defend a position, dug deep moats and fortified his ramparts; thus he caused his enemies to warn one another in fear, not daring to invade, while he himself remained clear and untroubled.
To destroy and crush [the enemy] was certainly not his primary concern. Alas! The appearance of the Venerable One in this world was of such great significance to the nation.
The movement of the Dharma proceeds in this manner. In this vast and distant world, it was only the Elder Master Hanshan who was able to know it and speak of it;

yet his composition of this stupa inscription has been like chewing tea-leaves and wax—something that remains between the teeth and tongue. As the saying goes: "I have heard there is such a thing as fate."
It was something I did not dare to tell others. In the year following the passing of the Venerable One, the Wanyili Basi year, I dreamed that I had reached a high mountain.
There sat a Great Monk in a precarious posture at the edge of a cliff; I recognized him as the Venerable Daguan.

After I had paid my respects by bowing at his feet, he pointed to a spot on the ground to my left and commanded me to sit there. He spoke to me in secret words of entrustment, exhorting me not to forget them, as he shed tears.

I woke with tears of sorrow. It has now been nearly sixty years since then. In my private reflections, I have long wished to follow in the footsteps of the Venerable Han (Zhuhong) to compose a second stele inscription, thereby continuing the *Monastic History* (*Sengshi*), corroborating the *National History* (*Guoshi*), and bringing to full light the splendor that remained unmanifest in the original epitaph.
Yet, as the days and months have passed, the atmosphere has grown dark and obscured. Sixty years have slipped away like a dream from the past.
I weep and lament for this world; I have already held my brush and set it aside for many years. It was not that I dared to break my word to the two elders.
Whenever I reflect upon myself, I am but a youth from the past who was unacquainted with the Buddha-dharma.
I know not by what causes and conditions I received a prediction of enlightenment in a dream. Now, with hair gone and brush worn out, I have achieved nothing. I follow the traces of my own past...
Counting the characters and arranging the surviving texts, like an elderly monk picking up stray letters from broken cages and old paper, I have made this my task wave after wave, kalpa after kalpa.
Might the Venerable One not smile at himself within the Constant Quiescent Light (*nityapraśānta-prabhā*), thinking that I have lost a pair of eyes?
Now that this separate collection is completed, I respectfully write these words following it to repent and restrain myself; perhaps there may be something for which to wait. Venerable One.
Regarding these writings—whether a single word or half a verse—they flow forth from the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Like mercury spilled upon the ground, every drop is perfectly round.
I do not dare to presume to sort or select them lightly; yet, those scattered throughout the collection are not few.

For instance, there is the "Discourse on the Exiled Guest" written in the year of Yiwu (1655) upon sending off the Venerable Han across the mountain pass, as well as the version seen by Gu Zhonggong in the manuscript held by Master Duanju Kai. These are all considered outstanding.

These various chapters of mine are truly the eyes of the Dharma gates. That the purple vapor between the stars has not vanished for so long—could this perhaps be an auspicious omen for these writings?
Although I am already advanced in years, I still wish to behold them.

A Brief Explanation of the Four Divisions of Ālayavijñāna: To investigate the mysteries of yin and yang, to encompass the essence of cosmic transformation, to penetrate the source of the vast nebula, and to break open the caverns of primordial chaos—
to transcend Confucianism and Daoism in solitary loftiness, and to crown all other schools with profound depth— none can achieve this except through the doctrine of Vijñaptimātra (Cognition-Only).
And as for seeking it [elsewhere], such has never existed. Now, by negating the existence of objects, consciousness is distinguished from the voidness of the mind.
By negating objects, there is no phenomenon outside of consciousness; by distinguishing it from voidness, it is not the same as a withered extinction.

Thus, the pits of eternalism and nihilism are leveled, the paths of arising and ceasing are blocked, the Middle Way is perfectly revealed, and the science of *hetuvidyā* (logic) is definitively established. Demons and heretics lose all hope, while both the ordinary and the holy alike follow it. However...
There are eight kinds of consciousness. Furthermore, there is the distinction between the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*).

Were it not for wisdom that is empty and luminous, and for contemplation that is subtle and profound, how could one easily peer into their inner courtyard? Regarding the *ālaya-vijñāna* and the others, I have roughly investigated the origins from which they arise.

It is simply that when True Suchness (tathatā) reaches its ultimate illumination, it conversely becomes obscured. When the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing are in union, this is called the "self-witnessing portion" (svasaṃvittibhāga).
It is like a person who has suddenly fallen into a stupor after being awake: although they hear the voices of others, they cannot comprehend them clearly.
If one says they are awake, they cannot comprehend clearly; if one says they are in a stupor, they still hear the voices of others. This is what is meant by "stupor-awakening."
These two aspects are intermingled; they are the very gateway between delusion and awakening. During such moments, if someone calls out to one, the state of darkness follows the emergence of clarity.
If no one calls, clarity follows the return to darkness. Once clarity has followed darkness, one cannot externally discern objects, nor does one internally dream;

there is only a state of profound obscurity. This is called the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (the self-verifying portion). During these moments, there is no distinction between subject and object; all is in profound stillness.
Yet it remains alone. After a short while, one suddenly dreams of all manner of sorrows and joys, sufferings and pleasures;
the capacity to observe and speak of them is called the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing-division). That which is observed is the *nimitta-bhāga* (the image-division). Someone may ask:
"Do these two divisions, the seeing and the image, arise sequentially, or do they arise simultaneously? I respond to this: To say that the two divisions of seeing and image arise sequentially—
Within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), non-conceptualization is not permitted; as soon as conceptualization arises, direct perception ceases.
This is called "antagonistic arising," wherein the subject and object are no longer identical. These four divisions are the foundation of the eight consciousnesses;

therefore, those who are intent upon this school must not fail to exercise careful attention. If these four divisions are thoroughly penetrated, then the framework of the eight consciousnesses will be understood. Reflect deeply upon this.
This is half [of the task].
A brief explanation of the first five consciousnesses:

Now, the eight consciousnesses and their four modes (catuskoṭi) constitute the skeletal framework of the *lakṣaṇa* school. [These include] the *ālayavijñāna*, the *manas-vijñāna*, and the [six] modes...
The distinct consciousnesses—eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness—are called the eight consciousnesses.

The self-witnessing division (*sākṣin-svabhāga*), the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), the seeing division (*darśana-bhāga*), and the image division (*nimitta-bhāga*) are called the four divisions. To speak of their fundamental nature:

these eight consciousnesses and four divisions originally possess no separate substance; they arise solely because True Suchness (*tathatā*) follows conditions, thereby manifesting in various forms. As for this True Suchness following conditions—
The meaning is most difficult to clarify. Often, both lecturers and Chan monks alike are unable to explain how it is that [the mind] "accords with conditions" (*suiyuan*).
This is because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is fundamentally pure and originally free from any taint; how, then, could it suddenly give rise to the process of acceding to conditions?
If one investigates this point without ceasing, a sudden awakening will occur. Thus, the so-called eight consciousnesses and four parts need not be troubled over.
With a little examination of the texts on Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra*), one will be able to understand them clearly. Therefore it is said:
if one masters the school of Nature (*Xingzong*) but does not master the school of Characteristics (*Xiangzong*), then what is seen by the school of Nature is still not complete.

If one masters the school of Characteristics but does not master the school of Nature, then what is seen by the school of Characteristics is likewise not refined or penetrating. Even if one masters both Nature and Characteristics, yet has not awakened to the Chan of Bodhidharma, then it is as follows:
Lord Ye painted a dragon; though its head and horns appeared undeniably lifelike from a distance, it was utterly incapable of ending a severe drought or summoning rain and thunder.

Therefore, when one aspires to transcend the world and shoulder the burden of the Dharma—whether regarding its nature (*svabhāva*), its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), or the Chan school—how could one not exert sincerity and devote oneself with focused attention?
Only the Abhidharma (the School of Characteristics) contains a vast number of names and definitions; if...
The subtle and profound mysteries of the mind and intellect cannot be fully elucidated through detailed and meticulous exposition; indeed, they are not easily clarified.
Now, I shall extract the general outlines and briefly discuss and annotate them, merely providing a rough understanding for the ignorant and childlike.

Generally speaking, the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) encompasses the preceding five consciousnesses—those of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—and should be explained in conjunction with them; this seems to make it easier to understand. For the *ālaya-vijñāna*...
The manas-vijñāna and the first five vijñānas both belong to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and both undergo transformation within the superior grade of fruition.

As for the seventh and sixth vijñānas, they possess all three grades. The three grades are as follows: the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is the inferior grade; the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is the middling grade; and the Ultimate Path (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) is the superior grade.

Therefore, the sixth and seventh vijñānas undergo transformation within the causal state. This is further analyzed according to the three objects, the three types of cognition, and the three measures.

Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the fifty-one types of mental factors (*caitta-dharma*): as for the first five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), their mode of cognition belongs exclusively to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and their objects belong exclusively to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
They are all permeated by the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral. As for the mental factors, there are only thirty-four. The verse says:
"Objects of the nature of reality, direct perception, and the three natures; The three [faculties] of eye, ear, and body abide in two stages. As for the universal [mental factors]..."

The objects of the wholesome consciousnesses are eleven; the intermediate [unwholesome] have two, while the great [neutral] have eight: greed, hatred, and delusion. The five sensory consciousnesses share the same support, which is the translucent material sense-faculties (*rūpaprasāda*).

Nine [consciousnesses] take seven as their objects; the seventh and eighth are adjacent to the "good" [objects]. Combining the three and separating the two, one contemplates the mundane world. The foolish find it difficult to distinguish between consciousness and the faculties.

Contemplating the transformation of appearances as empty occurs only through subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Even within the fruition, this does not yet fully describe the ultimate truth. When the perfect luminosity first arises, it becomes untainted (*anāsrava*).

"Three classes of transformation bodies cease the wheel of suffering. In this verse, the first eight lines clarify only that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), while the final four lines clarify that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*).

Furthermore, within the first eight lines, the first two lines refer to the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), whose three objects belong exclusively to the category of objective spheres (*viṣaya*).

Regarding the three types of objects: they are the objective realm (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), the object with a shared essence (*sābhāsa-viṣaya*), and the object as a solitary reflection (*pratibimba-mātra-viṣaya*). As for the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), these pertain exclusively to the objective realm;

however, all three types of objects are common to all three natures. Regarding the three types of valid cognition: they are direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), inference (*anumāna-pramāṇa*), and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Regarding the three natures: they are the wholesome nature, the unwholesome nature, and [the neutral nature].
Their nature is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, regarding these five consciousnesses in terms of their realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*):

in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), specifically the stage of the "mixed dwelling of the five destinies," all consciousnesses are fully present. However, in the First Dhyāna, the stage of "joy born of seclusion," the five consciousnesses are not complete.

From the Second Dhyāna upward, because applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) are absent, the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue do not arise. This is because in the heavens of the dhyānas, there are no material objects (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).

Because of food. Edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) has the three factors of odor, taste, and tangibility as its essence. Since edible food is absent, it is evident that these two consciousnesses do not arise.
There are many explanations regarding the meaning of direct perception (pratyakṣa). "Direct" (prati) means manifesting; it refers to the clear and immediate apprehension of an object.
"Perception" (akṣa) means measuring. When the mind and mental factors take an object, they are clearly manifest, free from obscuration and the like.

It is clear. One attains the self-nature of objects. That which is called "attaining the self-nature of objects" means that the fundamental objects (*dharmatā-viṣaya*)—the sense faculties and their objects—are constituted by eight factors.
Each possesses a real substantiality and an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*); each arises from a real seed; each possesses real functional efficacy;

and because they are presently existing real dharmas, they are precisely the *ālambana-vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only as the object). Furthermore, the present belongs to the object, while the measure (*pramāṇa*) belongs to the mind, or both may belong to it.

Regarding "mind" (*citta*): it may be explained through three grammatical analyses—*tatpuruṣa* (dependent), *karmadhāraya* (appositional), or *bahuvrīhi* (possessive)—depending on whether the measure belongs to the sense faculty (*indriya*) or to the mind itself.
In the West (India), there are six types of explanations for names: first, *tatpuruṣa*; second, *karmadhāraya*; third, *bahuvrīhi*; fourth, *dvandva* (contradictory);

fifth, *saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa* (with number); and sixth, *sāmīpya* (proximate). Furthermore, there is the *tatpuruṣa* analysis. These six analyses, when categorized by their combinations and separations, are essentially variations of these six [types] interacting with one another.

Because of the combination and separation [of words], each of the six types of analysis (*ṣaṭ-vyākhyāna*) possesses both names. If it were a single word, it would not constitute one of the six analyses, as it could not establish the characteristics of combination and separation.

Regarding the first, the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound): this means that the basis is taken as the primary element. For example, in the expression "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*), consciousness arises dependent upon the eye;
it is thus "the consciousness of the eye," and is therefore called "eye-consciousness. By citing the eye as the primary factor upon which the consciousness depends, it is so named.

Regarding "dependent designation" (*tatpuruṣa*), it is also called "dependent" (*bhartṛdārika*). This is like taking the name of a son based on his father; for example, "the father of such-and-such official, who is the elder brother of this person.
Furthermore, regarding "separation" (*viyoga*) and "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*): "separation" means that the eye is the faculty (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the act of discerning;

the faculty is not identical to consciousness, nor is consciousness identical to the faculty. Therefore, it is called "separation. "Conjunction," however, refers to calling them by the same name without distinguishing between the faculty and consciousness; therefore, it is called "conjunction. This is what is meant by "retaining" (*dhāraṇa*).

Regarding the term "function" (*karma*): as it is said concerning the *ālayavijñāna*, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to its essence (*svabhāva*), while "store" (*ālaya*) refers to its functional activity (*karman*).

Activity can manifest the essence, and the essence can sustain the activity; since the store is itself consciousness, it is called the "consciousness of sustained activity" (*ālambana-vijñapti-vijñāna*). It is also called the "consciousness of common support" (*samāśraya-vijñāna*).

"Store" refers to the function of containing and storing, while "consciousness" refers to the function of discerning and cognizing. These two share a single basis of support; therefore, it is called the "consciousness of common support. Thus it is said that there is...

Regarding "wealth" (*dhana*): it receives its name from that which is possessed. First, for example, *Buddha* means "the Awakened One"; because he is one who possesses awakening, he is thus named "Awakened.
This is a case of adopting a name derived from another. Second, for example, *Abhidharmakośa* is not itself the "Treasury of Abhidharma" (*Abhidharmapiṭaka*).
"Treasury of Abhidharma" is the title of the root treatise; because this work was composed based upon that fundamental Treasury of Abhidharma, it is so named.

Regarding the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, this title is taken entirely from another source. Furthermore, as for the meaning of "possessing wealth" (*sādhana*), how is it explained? As for "contradiction" (*viruddha*):

it refers to cases such as the eye and the ear, where each respective referent is independent and does not accord with the other; hence they are called "contradictory. As for "indicating number" (*saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa*):
it clarifies the meaning by means of a numeral, and applies to all three types of explanation, such as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the two truths (*dvaya-satya*).

The five are the aggregates (*skandha*); the two are the truths (*satya*). These take their own nature as their name; thus they are *karmadhāraya* (appositional) and *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compounds, such as the six consciousnesses beginning with the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), which take themselves and others as their names.
These are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) and *bahuvrīhi* compounds, such as when the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) are called the "five [types of] lack of learning" (*pañca-aśruta*).

Here, "immediate" (*ānantarya*) refers to the result; this is speaking of the cause by means of the result. This takes the name of another entirely; thus it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound denoting possession (*svasvāmisaṃbandha*).

Regarding the term "proximate" (*upaniṣad*), it is named according to its proximity. For example, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): they have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential nature, but because wisdom is proximate to mindfulness, they are called "foundations of mindfulness.

Since this is a case of being proximate rather than being named after its own intrinsic function, it does not carry the sense of a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). It admits of two other interpretations:
first, the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) of proximity, such as when someone lives near Cháng'ān and another person asks, "Where do you live? [The answer would be, "I live near Cháng'ān."]
The answer was, "I dwell in Chang'an. This person is not from Chang'an; it is because they are near Chang'an that they say they dwell in Chang'an.

This is a case of taking another's name as a partial designation. Furthermore, there are two types of proximity: proximity by way of dependence (*tatpuruṣa*) and proximity by way of possession (*bahuvrīhi*). It is like being asked, "Where are you from? and responding accordingly.

The answer was: "Chang'an. By using the name of another place to designate one's own name, it is called *yǒucái* (possessing wealth). Because it is near Chang'an, it is further named *línjìn* (adjacent). The verse says: Using one's own and using another's, Neither one's own nor another's, Pervading both, pervading three kinds— Such are the six modes of explanation. These six explanations are those that must necessarily be employed when commenting upon sutras and śāstras, as follows: 1. *Yǒucái* (Possessing Wealth): Using the name of another place to designate one's own location. 2. *Línjìn* (Adjacent): Using the name of a nearby place to designate one's own location. 3. *Zìyòng* (Using One's Own): Using the name of one's own location to designate one's own location. 4. *Tāyòng* (Using Another's): Using the name of another location to designate another location. 5. *Jùfēi* (Neither One's Own Nor Another's): Using neither one's own nor another's name to designate one's own location. 6. *Tōngèr* (Pervading Both): Using the names of both one's own and another's locations to designate one's own location.

7. *Tōngsānzhǒng* (Pervading Three Kinds): Using the names of three different locations to designate one's own location. These six modes of explanation are indispensable for the commentary of all sutras and treatises. As it is said: [The text continues with examples].
This commentary on the eight consciousnesses could not have been fully elucidated without this [text], which shall therefore be presented in systematic order.

The two lines beginning with "The five [consciousnesses] each have five" describe the mental factors (*caitta*) associated with the five sensory consciousnesses. Regarding these mental factors of the five consciousnesses, there are five universal factors; five object-specific factors; eleven wholesome factors;

two of the indeterminate (inherent) factors; and eight of the great ground-incongruous factors. Adding the three—greed, hatred, and delusion—to these, when taken together: (Note: The text here provides a structural outline for the subsequent classification of mental factors according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* system.)

Thirty-fourth: Regarding the statement that "the five consciousnesses share the same support in the pure material sense-faculties" (*rūpa-indriya*), this refers to the support of these consciousnesses as being not the physical, superficial faculties (*sāṃvṛtika-indriya*), but rather the ultimate, pure material faculties (*paramārtha-rūpa-indriya*). These faculties cannot be seen by the physical eye;

only those who possess the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) can perceive them. Regarding the phrase "the nine conditions for the seven and eight [consciousnesses] are favorably adjacent," this refers to the arising of the five consciousnesses.
Meaning: The five consciousnesses must rely upon nine conditions in order to arise. These nine conditions for the five consciousnesses are:

space, light, the sense organ, the object, attention (*manasikāra*), the supporting basis of discernment (*vikalpa-āśraya*), the supporting basis of defilement and purity (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-āśraya*), the fundamental supporting basis (*mūla-āśraya*), and the seeds (*bīja*). Regarding the statement "combining three and separating two when observing the sensory realm":

this refers to the two consciousnesses of the eye and ear, which apprehend their objects through separation; whereas the three [consciousnesses] of the nose, tongue, and body apprehend their objects through conjunction. This is the view of the ignorant.
Regarding the difficulty of distinguishing between consciousness and the faculties: this refers to the Śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle who follow the teachings of the ignorant.
They do not understand that both the faculties and consciousness each possess their own seeds and manifest activities; they falsely claim that the faculties and consciousness arise from one another.

While it may be said that the seeds and manifest activities of the faculties merely guide the seeds and manifest activities of consciousness—such that the faculties can be considered the conditions for the arising of consciousness—it cannot be said that the faculties themselves produce consciousness.
This is not possible. Since consciousness itself possesses the seeds capable of producing [itself], what else could serve as the seed that produces consciousness?

Therefore, those of the Hīnayāna have not yet eliminated the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); their wisdom is shallow and their minds are coarse, and thus they do not understand the nature of phenomena.

Consequently, they do not believe in the Mahāyāna teaching of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). These five consciousnesses are limited by being contaminated (*sāsrava*). As for the latter four lines, they clarify the absence [of such limitations].

This refers only to the meaning of "outflows" (*āsrava*). Regarding the statement that "transforming appearances to contemplate emptiness occurs only through subsequently attained cognition (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), and even within the state of fruition it does not directly designate the ultimate truth (*tattva*)," this refers to the followers of the Hīnayāna.
They claim that the five types of outflow-free consciousness (*anāsrava-pañca-vijñāna*) can transform appearances to contemplate emptiness. Therefore, the Mahāyāna masters refute them by saying:
"Even these outflow-free five consciousnesses, while in the stage of the Buddha’s fruition, cannot yet directly take *tathatā* (suchness) as their object; how much less [could they do so] otherwise?"
Regarding the phrase "In the causal stage, perfect luminosity first arises, accomplishing the outflow-free [wisdom], and the three types of transformation bodies cease the wheel of suffering":

this means that when the causal stage of the five consciousnesses is exhausted and the fruit is perfected, the associated mental factors collectively become the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is To Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

This wisdom manifests the three types of bodies to bring to rest the wheel of suffering for sentient beings. This is because, at the stage of Buddhahood, the eighth consciousness is transformed into the outflow-free state.
The pure white consciousness, subsequently associated with mental factors (*caitta*), immediately becomes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and manifests suddenly before one;
hence it is said that "it first arises. At this same time, the first five consciousnesses also transform their consciousness into wisdom.

Once the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) is attained, what difficulty could there be in manifesting the three types of emanation bodies? Regarding these "three types," they include the great transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of a thousand *zhang* in height, which...
The Bodhisattvas of the four stages of application (*prayoga*) of the Mahāyāna manifest a transformation body of one *zhang* and six *chi*.

They manifest according to the capacities of those in the three stages of the Mahāyāna provisions (*saṃbhāra*) as well as ordinary beings of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Thus, their manifestations universally reach all three vehicles, and all beings of the six realms equally transcend [suffering]. Someone may ask:

The first five consciousnesses achieve the mental states associated with outflow-free (anāsrava) wisdom and manifest in the present body to benefit sentient beings. Why, then, does the text first state that the eighth consciousness achieves outflow-free wisdom?
It is because the initial emergence of perfect luminosity occurs when the mental states associated with the eighth consciousness become the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna).

Furthermore, the first five sense organs are themselves the objective aspects (nimitta-bhāga) manifested by the eighth consciousness; since the fundamental consciousness that acts as the transformer [is the eighth], [it is through it that transformation occurs].
When [the consciousnesses] become untainted (*anāsrava*), the five faculties (*indriya*) they transform will naturally and immediately become untainted as well.

Since the five faculties that give rise to [consciousness] have already become untainted, the five faculties that are produced by them consequently become untainted. What room for doubt is there? Someone asks:

"It is said that the eight consciousnesses transform into the four wisdoms (*jñāna*); why then do you speak instead of the associated mental factors (*citta-dharma*)? I reply: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, chapter ten, states: [text follows].
These four categories collectively encompass all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) merits of the Buddha-ground without exception.

This transformation of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) mental states associated with the eight consciousnesses—the seventh, sixth, and five sensory consciousnesses—is attained respectively as wisdom (*jñāna*). Although this is not consciousness itself, it arises in dependence upon consciousness;

because consciousness is the primary factor, it is said that "consciousness transforms and attains" [wisdom]. Furthermore, in the contaminated state, wisdom is weak while consciousness is strong. In the uncontaminated state, it is the opposite.

Within the state of outflows (*āsrava*), wisdom is strong while consciousness is weak. To encourage sentient beings to rely on wisdom and abandon consciousness, it is said that consciousness is transformed into wisdom.
My initial statement that the eight consciousnesses and the five consciousnesses transform into wisdom should be annotated together; this is precisely that same meaning.

This commentary has already been seen in my collected works. Because the Great Master taught his disciples to study the Abhidharma (Saṃmitīya) school in depth, and because there are differences in detail and brevity among these versions, I have preserved them all here for reference.
The original commentary states: "This chapter provides the framework for the eight consciousnesses; more than half [of the essential meaning] has been considered.
The above was spoken by the Great Master while traveling in Dong'e for the benefit of Ruwen. At noon, he departed southward and did not finish the discourse.

Regarding the section on the eight consciousnesses and four divisions that follows, Ruwen later requested the Great Master to continue the explanation; however, he only remembered the portion concerning the first five consciousnesses.
Regarding the twelve-line verse:
"The transformation-body contemplates emptiness only through subsequent attainment;

even within the fruit, it does not yet fully express the ultimate reality"—these two lines have long been confused by those who eloquently discourse on the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics) school, because they fail to understand Sthiramati’s [intent].

This is merely because [the opponent's position] is refuted by the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the *Dharmapāla-śāstra*. Generally speaking, according to the school of Sthiramati, the Hīnayāna does not recognize the existence of the eight consciousnesses;
what they know of are only the six consciousnesses. Once these six consciousnesses have ceased, there appears to be no discrimination, and it functions as if it were direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

One might then claim that there is no further path to be advanced; yet one fails to realize that what is realized by the Hīnayāna is entirely ignorance—that is, the lack of awakening within the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Thus, Sthiramati falsely asserts that the untainted five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) within the causal stage are already capable of objective cognition.
If these five consciousnesses are examined from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, how could they possibly be untainted (*anāsrava*)?

Since they encompass the natures of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate, can it truly be called "untainted" simply because the coarse evils have been exhausted while the subtle evils still remain?
Can it truly be called "conditioned by suchness" (*tathatālambana*)? Therefore, Dharmapāla, the protector of the Mahāyāna, refutes this with two phrases. Dharmapāla’s intention is as follows:

The contemplation of emptiness through the transformation of appearances can only be achieved by the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Furthermore, this subsequently attained wisdom cannot be obtained during the causal stage;

it must await the transformation of the eight consciousnesses into fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) before this wisdom can be acquired. This is what is meant by "fundamental followed by the subsequently attained";

this is a matter pertaining to the fruition stage, not something to be realized during the causal stage. It is only upon reaching the fruition that this wisdom can manifest through the transformation of appearances.

Nor can it perceive the essence as its object. For instance, if fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is taken to be ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) to be provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), then while ultimate wisdom can take suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, provisional wisdom can respond to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Even if provisional wisdom, at the stage of fruition, is able to take suchness as its object, [it cannot do so directly].

It is merely a transformation of appearance and cannot take [the object] as its direct cognitive support (*ālambana*). Nevertheless, while these five and eight consciousnesses transform into wisdoms only upon the attainment of the fruit (*phala*), the sixth and seventh can transform even within the causal stage (*hetu*).
As Sthiramati states, it is also possible for the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) to take suchness (*tathatā*) as its object during the causal stage.
To maintain that the uncontaminated five sense-consciousnesses (*anāsrava-pañca-vijñāna*) are capable of taking [suchness] as their object is truly laughable.
The original note states: "When the five consciousnesses transform upon reaching the fruit, it is called the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

At that time, they can only take the manifestation of the aspect as their object and rely upon suchness (*tathatā*), but they do not directly perceive it. Therefore, Dharmapāla says that even when these five consciousnesses reach the state of fruition, they still do not themselves designate suchness.
How, then, could the five consciousnesses have directly realized suchness while in the causal stage? These are the two lines of the verse.
Thus, Dharmapāla brought forth the correct meaning to refute the doctrine of Sthiramati.
Regarding the verse spoken by Viśvabhū Buddha, it is as [explained] for Viśvabhū Buddha:
this refers to the "Omniscient One who is Sovereignly Awakened. Since he is one who is sovereignly awakened, what thing could there be...
These are indeed hindrances. Thus, for those who have not yet awakened, there is no escaping stagnation wherever they encounter things:

when seeing form, they are hindered by form; when seeing emptiness, they are hindered by emptiness. Suddenly there is a body, and one is hindered by the body; abruptly there is a mind, and one is hindered by the mind.
Hindered by the body, there arise birth, old age, sickness, and death; hindered by the mind, there arise joy and anger.

Sorrow and joy: thus, while revolving within a single radiance, they falsely manifest as opposing poles. Once these poles have been established, the state of total lack of autonomy reaches its zenith.
Birth is pressed by old age; old age is pressed by illness; illness is pressed by death; joy is pressed by anger; anger is pressed by sorrow;
and sorrow is pressed by joy. To be "pressed" means to be driven on by one another. Alas!

If birth were fixed and permanent, old age could not be forced upon it; if joy were fixed and permanent, sorrow could not be forced upon it. Because they are impermanent, their flow cannot be stopped.

Only those who possess the Way realize that the body is impermanent because it is composed of the four great elements; they realize that the mind is impermanent because it arises from preceding objects;
they realize that the four [elements] are impermanent because they depend on a single body; and they realize that objects are impermanent because they depend on the mind.

Because there is existence, one is used to dissolve the four; since the four have no standing, the four are used to dissolve the one. Since the one has nothing in which to abide, the one is used to dissolve the object;
yet the mind originally does not exist. The mind is used to dissolve the object, and the object naturally does not remain. One and four mutually dissolve; both mind and object are forgotten.
A single body becomes infinite bodies, yet the characteristics of the body are not destroyed. A single mind extends its concern throughout the myriad things.
Things. Within the space of a single inch held in one's breast, one proceeds from the lack of self-mastery of all things to the mastery of all things.

For one who attains this realization, a single kṣaṇa can transcend vast eons; yet if one has not attained it, the banner of liberation becomes nothing more than a walking corpse or a lump of flesh, and the bridge of wisdom turns instead into the waves of karma upon the ocean of suffering.
From antiquity to the present, the most eminent heroes and geniuses have shattered this—

The pivotal point has not been grasped. Although one’s merit may transcend the ages and one’s fame may illuminate ten thousand generations, there is no connection whatsoever with the fundamental matter.

Thus, at the time of birth, one is deluded by the experience of birth; at the time of aging, one is deluded by the experience of aging; at the time of illness, one is deluded by the experience of illness;

at the time of death, one is deluded by the experience of death; and during times of joy, anger, sorrow, or pleasure, one is deluded by the experience of joy, anger, sorrow, or pleasure. In this way, delusion succeeds delusion.
Delusion has no end to its days. Man is the spirit of all things, yet this spirit does not awaken; it continues its delusion and serves as the root of all dark karma.
Even when mountains are high and waters are deep, there is no time when they can be shaken or exhausted. How can those who possess even a slight knowledge of self-reflection fail to be afraid?
Furthermore, the spirit is like flowing, penetrating water, while delusion is like obstructed, solid ice. When there is penetration, [the ice melts].

When it encounters the square, it is square; when it encounters the circle, it is circular. If there were obstruction, the square would remain fixed as square and the circle would remain fixed as circular.
To be unhindered by squareness or circularity is called "vitality"; for squareness and circularity to have fixed limits is called "death.

Therefore, the Sage dwells within the square and the circle, yet neither the square nor the circle can obstruct him. Because he is unhindered, he is able to penetrate the sentiments of the world. Ordinary people...
This is not so. Seeing the square, one is deluded by the square; seeing the circle, one gives rise to attachment to the circle.
Thus, for the sage, it is dying that is life; for the common person, it is living that is death. Therefore, the sage calls them "living people," while the common person calls them "dead people.
Viewed from this perspective, since ancient times, those whom we call "living people" have been able to attain—

How difficult can it be? To become a sage is not hard; the difficulty lies in attaining spiritual penetration (*tōryō*). If one can indeed attain spiritual penetration, it is not only that body and mind both become spiritual;

on a grand scale, from the void and the heavens and earth to the profusion of all things, and on a minute scale, from a single mustard seed or speck of dust to a single hair or strand of fur—there is nothing that does not become spiritual.
This extends even to the Tripiṭaka and the Six Classics, the various schools of philosophers, and the crafts of the hundred artisans.

Because there is nothing it does not penetrate: when the body is realized as spiritually penetrating, no matter can obstruct it; when the mind is realized as spiritually penetrating, no principle can hinder it.
One transforms birth, old age, sickness, and death into supreme *nirvāṇa*, and turns anger, joy, sorrow, and pleasure into the realization of great *bodhi*.
*Nirvāṇa* and *bodhi* are attained through the body and the mind; if there were no body or mind, how could these two fruits be reached? Therefore it is said: "This body is..."
The mountain of worldly afflictions: this mind is a sea of mixed poisons. Once one realizes that the body is not the self, the mountain of worldly afflictions is itself a mass of merit.
When one realizes that the mind is like an illusion, the sea of mixed poisons is itself the nectar of *prajñā*. Man is the most spiritual being among all things;
yet if he does not value himself, he will willingly become a dead man rather than a living one—how lamentable!
A Text for Sending the Dragon Son Back to Tanzhe Temple:

The dragon son of Tanzhe has manifested extraordinary spiritual responses; his protection of the Dharma is most steadfast. In the year Dinghai, I was about to pay homage to the Great Being Samantabhadra at Mount Emei.
Reflecting upon the perilous journey across water and land, where the level and steep terrain could not be fathomed, I then addressed him:
"O Father Dragon, though I lack virtue, I am a disgraceful son of the Buddha. My journey lies near at hand; pray, lend me your aid.
Thereupon, he reached Longquan and stayed as a guest at Qingxuan Guan in Jinan. One night, he dreamed of a small green snake that slithered down the wall.
Shortly after, the attendant Kai arrived and said to him, "To dream of a snake and for it to appear here—how strange! He replied:
"The Master is taking his staff toward the West; this must surely be the arrival of the Dragon of Mount Yan to join the covenant.
From then on, at every meal, he would set aside a portion for the dragon offspring. These dragon children assisted him throughout his travels, changing with three cycles of cold and heat.

Treading upon waves and braving perils, they provided profound protection. In the year Jichou (1089), I finally returned eastward, entering the summer retreat at the residence of Inspector Yu in Qu'a.
At the villa, the dragon prince manifested his form and took leave of me, wishing to return to his former abode. Alas! The dragon is the sovereign among scaly creatures;
it can become large or small, and can remain hidden or manifest. Its wisdom, virtue, majesty, and spiritual power allow for manifold transformations, such as the many-headed, venomous Mānasvin;
the compassionate Nanda; the joyful Utpala; and the dark-hued Bhagīratha in the salt ocean.
These are all called "persons" (ren) either because of their virtue, their majesty, or their station; as for the dragon-like virtue [of these beings], it is beyond my knowledge.
The Great Blue and Little Blue dragons of Tanzhe are likewise of the dragon clan; they obey the commands of the Tathāgata to serve as guardians of the monastery.

Though possessing the form of snakes, they harbor the heart of a Buddha; though their species differs [from humans], they are steadfast in goodness. They do not fear people when seen, nor do they harm creatures when encountered. Year after year...
Or, when rain and sunshine fail to arrive at their proper times and the hundred grains wither, causing farmers to be filled with grief and alarm, the Two Blue Ones manifest their traces:

they spit forth clouds and spray their tears as thunder. In the mere twinkling of an eye, moisture drenches the great earth; that which was parched suddenly revives, and that which was prostrate rises up.
Those who had been frowning in distress now dance and rejoice. Thus, moved by the grace of the Blue Ones, [the fields] turn gold and azure.
His palace is magnificent and vast; his spirit endures through the ages, with inscriptions and records established to ensure he is never forgotten—this is the way of ritual propriety (*li*).

My Way is not sufficient to overcome my habitual training, yet as I traveled ten thousand *li*, I exerted myself for the sake of the Son of the Dragon; he remained tranquil and did not complain of fatigue, which may truly be called the exhaustion of one’s full strength.

How could I dare not personally visit the imperial court with these meager offerings to respectfully present them to the Father of the Dragon, so that the noble Son might be returned? I fear that if I delay, it will be too late.
The world does not recognize the virtue of this dragon; I shall briefly record it so that it may be transmitted for eternity.

I further pray that the elders and juniors of this dragon lineage, by relying upon the blessed majesty of the Buddha, may attain the path of unsurpassed enlightenment and serve as a great golden fortress for all time.
Written on the second day of the fifth month of summer in the Renchen year of the Wanli era by the monk Daguan Ke.
The roads of Shu have been celebrated since antiquity as perilous and extreme; its peaks and crags stand sheer like pillars, and the Gorges of the Yangtze and Han swirl like boiling water.
Were it not for the assistance of divine power, one could not avoid being struck with terror. Yet when our Great Master visited Mount Emei, his traces were like those of clouds and water;
indeed, he traveled back and forth, riding upon calm currents and treading upon level paths. Is this not merely the mundane affair of a Perfected Being? And yet—
The Dragon Son of Tanzhe’s merits cannot be denied. At times he appeared as a youth to provide advance warnings;
at other times he manifested a great hand to rescue those in perilous rapids. When the Great Master was staying at Qu’a during the summer, the Dragon Son appeared in his usual form to take his leave.
How could one not understand such deeds? Having settled by the eastern gully, I came to cherish the sound of its waters, which spread far and wide.
Tongue! Why do you not recall how your Great Master, in years past, assembled the multitude to preach the Dharma? Here, you have instead spoken of two green spirits of wondrous appearance.
Furthermore, I have heard that the Dragon Prince attended his travels on Mount Emei; thus I have these words: "The spring water remains undiminished beyond the dust of the world;
the *bìluó* vines still hang upon my former robes. When the crane comes from Jǔqū, the clouds wait for him first. The Dragon...
Regarding the line, "Leaving Mount Emei, the rain has not yet ceased," I recently read the "Farewell to Longzi" and learned that Longzi was fully aware of it.
As you are about to depart, I have composed this poem to see you off: Soughing are the rains and mists; The wind blows the tree leaves to fall.

As I traveled down from the northern mountain, sitting there I beheld the little dragon returning. The snow-capped cliffs of Shu were draped with pearl nets; the river clouds guarded his precious robes.
One may know that the power of the Dharma has reached him, as the terraces and halls now unfold in radiant splendor. Alas!
I had hoped to see the Dragon Son between the tongs and ladle of the furnace, yet the Dragon Son now returns to his native mountains while I still linger in the land of illness. Your disciple, Ru.
Peng respectfully appends this postscript:

The *Shuo yuan wei xia hun san zhi zhui lun* (The Original Axle-Wheel for the Dharma-Assembly of Smelting Away Dullness and Scattering) at Tianchi Mountain is that which the Buddhas of the three periods have transmitted to one another in succession. However, as for...
It simply depends on how one employs it. If employed skillfully, it dispels delusion and distraction in a single instant and sustains *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within great quiescence.
It causes mountains and rivers to vanish into the ground where they have never existed; it washes away body and mind in the realm of non-attainment.

It is the sharp blade that severs the fetters of desire and the support for the right livelihood of the spiritual body. It manifests the courageous heart of those who see the truth, as one wanders through the realm of the Elephant Emperor.
Originally, there was a divine pearl whose radiance rested in the palm; it was never any other treasure, yet who could offer a price for its worth?

By means of the ordinary body one realizes the Buddha-body; relying on conventional truth, one constructs ultimate truth. Its merit fills space and bestows freely; its virtue is abundant and immeasurable.

Truly, when a practitioner’s single breath is cleared of dullness and distraction, that very breath is the Buddha; when a single thought is cleared of dullness and distraction, that very thought is the Buddha.
O Buddha! Alas! Within this vast and boundless sea of suffering, there are those with breath and blood who do not lack a spiritual essence, yet they rise and sink like waves beyond counting.

Suppose there were a single person who, beneath the hammering wheel [of karma], could purify even one breath and one thought of delusion and distraction to achieve one breath and one thought of mindfulness of the Buddha—if one were to observe this with the Buddha-eye, then...
The merit of this is truly inconceivable; how much more so for those who practice for many days! Indeed, a person values self-reflection.
If one can truly reflect back upon the state of one's own mind—its dullness and distraction—from birth until death, has there ever been a single kṣaṇa in which these have ceased?
Therefore it is said: "If a person sits in stillness for even a single moment, it surpasses the construction of stupas made of the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

These stupas will ultimately turn to dust, but a single thought of stilling the mind achieves perfect enlightenment. Even if one does not apply this skillfully, one will at least not lose the field of merit for humans and devas.
For this reason, those who are wise—whether monastics or laypeople, noble or common, and those capable of eloquent speech—should propagate and praise this; those with power [should likewise do so].

Those who encounter this should protect and uphold it, providing for its needs in every way. All those at sites such as meditation halls (daochang) should assist in its propagation with impartial hearts.
This text has already been included in the Complete Collection. As for the Tianchi Meditation Hall, even to this day it remains occupied by demonic outsiders.
Thus, whenever members of the fourfold assembly—monastics and laity alike—pass through this place, none fail to feel sorrowful in their hearts; therefore, I have selected and recorded this account.
The characters for "Chishan Daochang" (Pool Mountain Practice Site) and so forth serve as the eyes for the people of this world. May those who behold them take care to look closely.
On the day of the winter solstice in the year of Gengzi, written respectfully by the Elder Qianyi.
Preface to the Lankavatara Sutra Carved by Mr. Bao The body is not itself the body;
it is the body because of the mind. The mind is not itself the mind; it is the mind because of the body. Because of the mind there is the body, yet the body cannot be apprehended.
Because of the body there is the mind, yet the mind also cannot be apprehended. Since both body and mind cannot be apprehended, [they are ultimately non-existent].
Then the mountain of wisdom stands solitary and the ocean of awakening is clear and still; the paths of emotional consciousness are exhausted, and subject and object are stilled and severed.
If this is so, not only can sentient beings not go there, but even those possessed of great supernormal powers—how could they possibly go?

This sutra takes the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness as its core tenets, and it explains them directly for Bodhisattvas whose faculties are mature.

When the substance of consciousness is entirely true, it immediately becomes the function of wisdom. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that this place is "inaccessible," which signifies the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground;

it cannot be entered through cultivation or realization. Therefore, any reader of this scripture who can directly and thoroughly penetrate it—finding no path for body or mind and no gate to self-nature—then a common person in a physical body may go there immediately. De Taishi said to me:
He said, "The newly carved edition of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra by Bao-sheng has calligraphy that is refined and concise, clear and brilliant.

It causes those who behold it to have their minds opened and their vision clarified. I beg the Master for a word to serve as the vanguard for its circulation; what do you think? For this reason, I wrote this.

Preface to a Brief Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom The great treatise of the *Prajñāpāramitā* consists of millions of words; like the surging waves of the vast ocean, it is boundless and unfathomable.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva, out of his compassionate grace, condensed its breadth into a concise form, resulting in this *Heart Sūtra*. Its language is essential and succinct, yet its profound purport is entirely complete within it.
From the Tang dynasty until the present, commentaries and sub-commentaries have appeared in great numbers. Eminent scholars and profound masters have, in turn, caused the divine resonance to vibrate;

yet the karmic conditions for their reception were never fixed, and preferences varied without constancy. As some adopted this while rejecting that, there arose mutual gains and losses, leaving later generations with lingering doubts that became manifold.

I showed Bao Sheng that when the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* speaks of "the single mind not arising," it asks, "What fault can there be in the myriad dharmas? *Śūraṅgama* means that all phenomena are ultimately firm and solid.

Observing this very point: the discernment of wisdom is proximate to the mind and its principle is ultimately firm; the meaning of the Tathāgata is proximate to phenomena and its reality is ultimately firm.
Why is this? When sentiment arises, wisdom is obstructed. If the single mind does not arise, is this not the state before sentiment has arisen?
If sentiment has not yet arisen, there is no phenomenon that is not ordered, and no phenomenon that is not known by wisdom. Therefore, I say: it is the discernment of wisdom.
The intent of the former [Xuefeng] approaches the ultimate of principle (*li*), while that of the Tathāgata approaches the ultimate of phenomena (*shi*).

In the past, Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying, "Those two monks truly act for the sake of others. Xuansha said, "A divine light shines ten thousand miles from behind his head," and he also said, "The skull is itself the adamantine body (*vajra-kāya*).
Are these not all examples of the firm and solid nature of the ultimate of phenomena? Bao Sheng indeed...
If you can realize it within the phrases of intellectual discernment, you have not yet glimpsed it even in a dream within the phrases of the Tathāgata.
If you can realize it within the phrases of the Tathāgata, you have not yet glimpsed it even in a dream within the phrases of Xuefeng and Xuansha.

If you can penetrate all various phrases without obstruction, then the ten fascicles of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, from beginning to end—proceeding from characters to accumulate into phrases, and from phrases to accumulate into...

The accumulation of phrases is like a horizontal axis upon which one presses down and drags upward; whether coarse or refined, with mind or without mind, there is nothing that is not ultimately firm and solid.

If you have not yet been able to penetrate thoroughly through various phrases, it does no harm to maintain the practice morning and evening, in honor and in disgrace, with eyes open and eyes closed, while defecating and urinating, and while dressing and eating—maintain it. Maintain it.

Bring it here and hold it; hold it when alive and hold it when dead. Hold it once every day. Once it is matured, the skull will throb and leap, emitting vajra-light and forming a sun and moon like an inverted basin.

What could be more appropriate? If one recites the sutras but does not follow this method of holding them, how is that different from a spring bird chirping by day or an autumn insect crying out at night? Let the student Bao exert himself in this.
The monk Bázào wrote out the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in ink.

During the early years of our dynasty, the Bodhisattva Yǐnshān Lóng, while still a youth, transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, each in one volume, using his own blood.

Later, when the August Emperor established the custom of testing candidates for the ordination of monks, there were those whose mastery was not refined who nonetheless falsely presented themselves for the examination.

The Emperor was enraged. He sentenced the presiding monk and three thousand others to serve in the military in remote border regions. Master Long went specifically to the capital, vowing to burn his own body to atone for the sins of the monks.
The Emperor granted his request and commanded the relevant authorities to establish a ritual site and provide strict security. The Master leaped joyfully onto the pyre.
When his body was half-consumed by the flames, he still wrote the four characters "Wind and rain shall be harmonious" with his own hand amidst the fire, leaving them as his final instruction.
The inner attendant said, "Wait until there is a drought, then burn it. Later, a severe drought indeed occurred. When the Emperor burned it, rain fell copiously and sufficiently.
The Emperor said, "This is the 'Ever-Abundant' rain (Yonglong). Alas! When Master [Dao]long was transcribing the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras with his own blood, [this occurred].
