When the mind is raised to draw blood, the Bodhisattva has already manifested his form; it is like a thick cloud parting, and the jewel-moon suddenly appears.
Waiting for you to open your eyes, the clouds gather and the light is missed. This light of bliss does not truly exist; how could suffering be retained?

The six sense faculties have both delusion and awakening; suffering and pleasure arise from them. By employing skillful means to uproot even one faculty, all sensory objects are simultaneously liberated.
A single speck of dust adheres to the essence of consciousness, obstructing every sense faculty. Inferring from this, if I wish to escape suffering and hardship, I must sever my own doubts;
the power of a Bodhisattva has no part in it.
In praise of the Maiden of the Horse-herd:

The fire of desire burns the spiritual root; the sprouts of the mind are ultimately scorched and extinguished. When the wise hear these words, their grief penetrates to the very marrow of their bones.
Alas for the people of the world, who regard such a flower-like woman as a treasure, hoping to sleep with her arm as a pillow—even death would be sweet to them!
The Bodhisattva deeply commiserates them. He manifests this subtle and wondrous form to cause sentient beings to see it with joy. From joy arises affection; from affection arises awakening;
and awakening gives rise to shame and remorse. Thus, they distance themselves from all women, becoming no different from the Bodhisattva himself.

Do not give rise to such impure thoughts regarding the body of a Bodhisattva. Humans are the most spiritual among all things; pigs and dogs are not even their equal. Because of this, lustful thoughts arise;
one must exert oneself to restrain them forcefully. Through diligent effort, one reaches the state of spontaneity, finally ascending to the ground of desirelessness.
Free from desire, they are the sages; they are eternally the sons of the Tathāgata. In this world, they act as the sun and moon, shattering the darkness of the great night.
When a single person perfects these virtues, the great trichiliocosm receives their benefit. These are the emanations of Avalokiteśvara; body after body, they are inexhaustible.
This eulogy for the image of the Great Being: Second Lord painted this image; Shifu received this image; and I too offer this eulogy for it.

Before it was painted, before it was received, and before it was eulogized, its perfect penetration was peerless from time immemorial. It is only because sentient beings give rise to fleeting emotions that daily life becomes so turbulent.

Sinking into gain and loss, one contemplates the wondrous form of the Honored One Avalokiteśvara. Ghostly faces and divine heads lose their original forms; when examining the state of mind, from where can difficulty arise?
Wicked men and fierce beasts are all teachers and friends; the fiery pit and the mountain of knives are gates of liberation.
The cawing of crows and the chirping of magpies enter into quiescence. Whether Confucian, Buddhist, or immortal, it is like the moon’s reflection appearing in clear water. Facing [this],...
Jie’s staff and Deshan’s shout—this is the broad and long tongue of Avalokiteśvara. When meeting one another, do not say, "I am still and silent.
A drop of water from a willow branch moistens parched thirst. But tell me, who knows its cold or warmth? Wait until you have tasted it for yourself; then it will not be too late to have it explained.
In praise of the Guanyin with Drooping Fingers:

The withered wood is not even a foot long; who could wield the hand of Prajñā to carve this subtle and wondrous form? The eyebrows and eyes are like mountains and seas—vastly extended yet profoundly still.
The facial features resemble the moon, its radiance illuminating this turbid world. Such is the scale of the body and the folds of the robes.
Full and heavy yet ethereal; the palms drape with *tūla* cotton, and the feet rest upon waves of lotuses.
In the place where not even a single thought has arisen, there is the form of a hand that has no hand. Thus, when a single finger falls away, all ten thousand phenomena fall away as well.
Among the hundred insects, none is more venomous than the Mahoraga;
with the body of a serpent and the head of a beast, it is difficult for either the holy or the mundane to categorize. It is like the long snake and the great boar.
The serpent and the scorpion—these are all considered venomous by the world; their poison is as fine as a hair. Among poisons, the most potent is that of the mahoraga.

Once they receive a prediction of enlightenment, they become the Buddha’s claws and fangs; whenever a Brahma-world is invaded, they slay the invaders with their poison, hearing the cries of suffering from the multitudes.

Observing with his eyes beneath the coiled pines, he bestowed compassion upon that place of venom. Manifesting a subtle and wondrous countenance, those who beheld him were transformed in their habitual tendencies.

As these tendencies shifted, consciousness was transmuted; the light of wisdom shone brilliantly as he harnessed great compassion to deliver all from the perils of poison. He held an axe while wearing a helmet.
Leaning against a pine tree in leisure, benevolent yet capable of valor, amidst springs and rocks, I bow my head to the Great Being. I take refuge in the Holy Avalokiteśvara.

*Praise of the Flame-Avalokiteśvara (with Preface)* All five metals and eight minerals can be transformed when they encounter fire; how much more so wood? Only the Sage is truly able to harmonize all things.
All things are one with the self; thus, water does not wash water, and fire does not burn fire.
One who understands this may be spoken with regarding the subtlety of the contemplation of fire. I bow my head in praise, saying:

The myriad things have no inherent substance; the mind alone is their foundation. Do not be deluded by this. That which is near can serve as that which is distant. Fire, fire—how could it not become water?
If one recklessly calculates transformation, a bowstring may be fashioned into an arrow.

In the *Guanyin Zan*, it is said that with a single eye one perceives all people of the world. These are the billions of minds, which constitute the billions of dharmas. Dharmas return to the One; the One returns to spontaneity (*ziran*);
spontaneity returns to non-existence. To speak of its subtlety, it encompasses as many grains of sand as there are in the Ganges River. To speak of its...
On a grand scale, they fill the ten dharma-realms.
Venerable Pindolabharadvaja (painted by Ju Dingyun and Peng): his shoulders are so high they are useless, serving only as a support for his staff;
his knees are likewise spacious, capable of holding the scriptures—what ailment could he have? Do not disdain the length of his eyebrows.
Fluttering over the rock grottoes, they do not obstruct the eye’s gaze;
as still as a cold pool, the second, Vakkula,
leans on his staff and extends his fingers— neither three, nor more than two— with leather covering his feet, yet the leather is loosened at the ankles, his air of refinement relaxed and leisurely.
Between the hermitages of Chao and You, his beard and hair remain as they were;
even his nostrils have long since been pierced by gnats. The third, Vakkula, has arched brows and bright eyes;
he waves his finger with serene detachment. This very hand is his tongue, its Dharma moistening humans and devas. Who could possibly be a tiger cub?
His fangs and claws are sharp; though he possesses them, he does not display them.
The jackals avoid him in fear. Fourth is the Venerable Subhūti:
his robe does not cover his chest; his mind is like empty space. Who would strike one who holds his fist? His mouth opens and lets the wind escape; it is said that he rests his hand upon his knee.
The knees have no self or person. This means that when the knees support the hands, the hands originally belong to the body.

Fifth, if the Venerable Nārada’s back truly existed, it would be difficult to relieve an itch by scratching it; yet since there is indeed no back, the scratching of the itch is not false. Thus he investigated back and forth.
Sentiments withered and wisdom exhausted; the pond is formed and the moon arrives. Seeing the Buddha before one's eyes—this is the Sixth Venerable Bhadra.
His head resembles a strange rock, his floating hair is like willows, and he holds a rosary in one hand. Using the rosary as a mouth, do not be startled by his broad chin.
Detailed yet intermittent; the Buddha’s head is inverted. Vaguely resembling Deshan, the seventh, Kālika, has a face as round as a plate.
His five sense organs are merged into a single orifice. He carves out his own domain and boundaries; he floats the pestle and sheds blood—the sovereign of the various schools.
His eyebrows should not be among the common; when sitting, they hinder the curvature [of his gaze], and when walking, they trail like clouds.
Eighth, Vajraputra (Vaśalavata) Honored One:
his robes fall from his shoulders as he emerges. His azure eyes are fixed upon the sutra. This sutra is most profound—a thunderclap within a great dream. These written characters are not the reality.
In truth, this is not of words. Standing alone with one foot extended, his two hands move freely.
The Venerable Bhagava of the Ninth Precept has no boundary behind his crown;
his forehead rests against a high crag. What he grasps in his hand is a fan that contains the dust of the world within its case; like surging clouds, he is free from intentional thought.
Occasionally veiling half the face, who would prostrate? Seeing directly yet not seeing;

the tenth, the Venerable Upagupta, gazes at the sutra with his head bowed, his shoulders and back swallowing his ears. A spring emerges from within the earth, serene upon the paper. The Old Lu of Lingnan.
The firewood load is temporarily set down; the mind that dwells nowhere is attained through this sutra.
The Venerable Rāhula’s hair bristled upward in rage, yet the Master alone was not thus.
Heeding the cutting of the *máoyīn* grass, his single anger was entirely dispelled; three times he yielded and twice he extended himself.
Rolling and unrolling with a single hand, he performs the Buddha-work of anger; truly an uninvited friend.

The twelfth, Venerable Nāgasena, supports his chin with both hands, fearing it might fall to the ground; his mouth is open and his teeth bared, his eyes bulging as his mind sleeps. His mind asleep, his body is forgotten.
The stone offers no resistance to its hardness; the stone forgets my feet. What harm is there in sinking into it?

The thirteenth [verse] concerns how Venerable Kātyāyana used his own forearm as a staff and held a rosary in his hand. Fearing further that his mind might wander, he leaned upon the sutra for his own amusement. Autumn skies, the cry of wild geese.
The Sanskrit characters were irregular; using these to praise the Buddha, the Elder Vana-vāsi, whose years had matured, understood them at once.

He remained with his mind in non-arising. I then entered my grotto in the cliff; the ripples formed patterns upon my robes, the spring sang amidst the verdant crags, and though my eyes did not open, [I perceived it all].
The light illuminates the six directions; brightness and darkness are both forgotten.
The essence of seeing is not mixed with anything else.

The fifteenth, Venerable Āśvaghosa, draws his shoulders together and clasps his knees, as if he were contemplating something. That which I contemplate is the mind-essence that has transcended thought; having transcended thought, he sits.
Broad or narrow, both are acceptable. The stone has no fixed form; the "blow-off-blade" sword leaves nothing to hide. The sixteenth note:
Venerable Upacāra (Half-Tongue) finds flowers blooming on a withered log.
It is not that the ears do not see. The forehead and nose both jut forward; how boundless is the springtime! Extension and contraction follow their constant laws.
The pivot is cut off, suppressing and uplifting; three straight lines and two curves. The arms and shoulders are grand and imposing.
The seventeenth, Venerable Qingzhi, takes lapis lazuli as his crucible;
within and without, all is transparently clear. His gaze is fixed upon its center; Mount Wutai appears before him. White clouds unfurl and roll away.
With a hundred forms and a thousand moods, they bury themselves at the roots of pine trees to manifest their sovereign freedom.

(18) Venerable Piṇḍola rests his staff against his forehead, making the forehead a stand for the staff; one shoulder towers alone, and both feet are set together as the price. Thus, the staff and the forehead differ.
What merit do host and guest possess? It lies solely in the shoulders and feet. To strike emptiness against the void—this is the self-praise of the leather-ball practitioner.
You, man, were not born into a famous or ancient clan; your disposition is for the most part broad, simple, and resilient.
Regarding the scriptures of both the mundane and supramundane worlds, he views them as if drinking fine wine that leaves one unawakened;

at times, he cannot find even a single word or character within his breast. As for the karmic conditions and entanglements of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, he exclusively delights in manipulating the theme of impermanence, remaining entirely without attachment.
At other times, he may resent the Buddhas and Patriarchs as lacking spiritual efficacy, casting them behind his head to indulge his own waywardness.

A single tongue. He disparages both sages and ordinary people. Suddenly he places a maggot from the toilet upon the crown of Vairocana; suddenly he casts the old fellow Bodhidharma to the leeward side.
He demands that others learn what is good, yet his own transgressions return to him like an echo. When a single word does not accord with his will, he treats princes and lords as spit.
"I look at you, a wretched life, tossing it here and there—why are you in such a hurry? *Du!* (A shout of rebuke)
To offer this body and mind to every dust-mote world—this is what is called being an enemy of the Buddha.
Second: A good friend has never investigated even one [principle]; they are not mature in the scriptural teachings and have not mastered a single treatise. Every time they encounter the absence of...
The Buddha stands supreme; yet suddenly one stumbles upon a fellow who has pierced his nostrils toward the heavens and planted his heels firmly on the ground.
I shall seize him by the collar and throat and cut off his tongue. I wonder where you will go next to exercise your wits?
Heh! When meeting, do not say there are no stratagems; these many snares and traps delude and confuse people.

I praise myself for having traveled as a wandering monk for over thirty years. I have traversed mountains and seas, sleeping under the open sky and eating what the wind brings. At Mount Emei, I was worn out by the thick white clouds;
at Potalaka, I cast aside the light of time. What has been accomplished? My hair has turned white and is difficult to turn back to black; the task remains unfinished.

Having understood this, my heart is filled with sorrow. But tell me: for what matter do you grieve? In the land of the Three Buddhas of Yongdong, the sea is vast and the fish and dragons reek of raw flesh;
at Tiantong and Xuedou, the Dharma drum has never sounded. With deep resolve, they serve every dust-mote world; the two Lis hear the sound with their eyes.
Li Cide Ji of Siming, together with his elder brother Licong Lin, collaborated on the design and execution of the painting of the Great Image.
He considered this to be the most divine likeness he had ever produced in his life; even down to the nails, hair, skin, and flesh, nothing was not rendered with perfect fidelity.
The Great Master himself wrote a eulogy for it, the calligraphy of which is magnificent and grand; it is currently preserved in the home of Lu Fu of Yongdong.
The eulogy for General Guan of Hanshou Ting:
The light of today was revealed at the time of hunting the deer at Xutian; the light of hunting the deer at Xutian was revealed on the day of the Peach Garden Oath.
This light and this heart further received the fragrance of the *Zuo Zhuan*, which they expanded and embodied within themselves.

The efficacy of practicing with vigor is indeed worthy of all ages. Like thunder and lightning, like the sun and the moon, it awakens those who are dormant in ignorance and shatters all profound darkness.
How virtuous is Shouting! For this reason, I praise him.
Eulogy for the Portrait of General Yue Fei of the Song Dynasty:

The brilliant glory of this general is peerless throughout all eternity. He learned archery from his teacher; though the teacher has passed away, he remains as if present before him. To serve his sovereign with such devotion—this is what defines him.

I dare not cherish my own life; though our paths of action differ, my single-minded resolve remains unwavering. The Central Plains have lost their strategic advantage, and the great villain is a source of loathing.
Occupying our borders, he has gathered his dog-like and sheep-like hordes in droves. May the General rouse his wrath to sweep away this stench and filth, restoring the Divine Land.
On the verge of accomplishment, it was abandoned; in my heart, I knew the treachery of [Wang] Gui. Yet, unable to turn my back on the sovereign’s command, I faced death as if returning home.

Serene and without regret, his brilliance is like that of the sun and moon, shining resplendently upon the Great Earth. Whether one is wise or foolish, who would not look up to him with veneration? At the pinnacle of Western Zhejiang—
This empty vessel is like a cauldron; within it lies a refined hermitage. The mountains and cities rest upon it; General, do not decline. Forever serve as a puppet for the Dharma:
those who are auspicious shall be granted blessings, while those who are calamitous shall be crushed to pieces. I ride upon the Buddha’s compassion and command you not to retreat.
The laywoman of Wujiang, Mother Zhou (née Lady Xue), praised [her] thus:
"Han Gaozu was of great magnanimity and Xiang Yu was fierce and violent; yet even at the moment of parting from life and death, they could not escape the sentiments of children.
Furthermore, those who have refined their meditative contemplation for twenty or thirty years amidst green mountains and white clouds may sit and pass away at the end of life."

Even such [attainments] are not easily found; how much less so for women? Throughout her life, Lady Ru had served the Buddha with exceptional diligence and faith in the Dharma-gate of Rebirth in the Pure Land.

Therefore, at the time of her death, although her household affairs were still being managed by her own hands and her children and grandchildren were gathered before her, she was entirely free from worldly attachments.
She passed away while sitting in a state of transcendence. Judging from this, the Lady far surpassed both Emperor Han Gaozu and Xiang Yu.
Some might say that for a woman of the inner chambers to be praised by a high monk is no empty boast. Alas! "Eternally cloudless is the moon over the Wu River;
in the Pure Land, lotuses bloom with the fragrance of the burning house."
Verses Presented by the Two Xings of Xunyang (from Wang Yutai’s *Bichu*).
While the Venerable Zibo was in Xunyang, the two lay practitioners Xi Laici and Kuangshi asked him in unison: "Qin..."
"General Bai Qi once slaughtered four hundred thousand people in a single day.

Because many people killed one person, and one person repaid the many, was it because the sins of the many were so heavy that the heavenly deity caused them to be slaughtered? These two doubts are entangled, contending within my breast.
I only pray that the Venerable One will resolve my perplexity and suddenly cleave through my accumulated defilements. The Venerable One then spoke this verse: "In the past, many were slaughtered..."

One. Now, where there was once one pit, there are many; one contraction and one extension, like the tips of arrows meeting. Fundamentally, there is nothing lost. Where there is no loss, there is no doubt.
Since doubt does not exist, what is there to be resolved? Use this to seal the mind. To claim that Heaven sends down irrationality is a mere sentiment; it exists emotionally but not in principle.
Emotion is like a dream, while the limit of principle is not a dream. Within a dream, there may be one or many, but upon waking, one traces back [the source].

Consider this: what is "many" and what is "one"? If one were to depart from even a single moment of thought, then distinctions between the many and the one—whether regarding the vastness of antiquity or the brevity of the present—would be obscured by intoxicated passions and a failure to perceive the underlying principle.

To fail to employ *anumāna* (inferential cognition) to reach a balanced resolution, to obstinately oppose the sagely judgment, and to engage in forced, arbitrary speculations, constitutes an irrational inquiry for which the wise do not provide an answer.
I pity those who are thus as if foolish; I have therefore forcibly composed these verses. From this day forward, do not give rise to such [views].

I see it. You must, before the Buddha, repent and wash away the defilements of ignorance; then merit and wisdom will grow in secret harmony. If you do not painfully reform yourself, you will ultimately become a follower of Māra or a heretic.
If my words are not true, may my tongue rot.
Reading the "Inscription on Dream Hall" (Mèngzhāi míngjì) by Dongpo (from *Wáng Yùtài’s Bǐchǔ*):
The Layman Dongpo said, "The minds of worldly people exist because of sensory objects (*rajas*); they have never existed independently.

The arising and ceasing of these objects does not abide for even a single thought-moment. Between dreaming and waking, object after object is transmitted; after several transmissions, one loses its [original nature]."
This is fundamental. Thus, one might think that form and spirit do not meet; is this not due to causal conditions? There was a man who was tending sheep and returned home.

Because of the sheep, he thought of horses; because of the horses, he thought of chariots; because of the chariots, he thought of canopies. He subsequently dreamed of a curved canopy and the sound of drums and pipes, and his body became that of a prince or high official.
Now, tending sheep and being a prince or high official are worlds apart; yet what the thoughts were conditioned by—was it not so?
How truly strange! The Elder Zibo stayed in my quarters and read with me the "Inscription on the Dream Chamber," then showed me this verse:
"When the eyes are open, mountains and rivers are seen; When the eyes are closed, mountains and rivers are seen. Since the seer is fundamentally one, How could that which is seen be two?
Though dream and waking are distinguished, The seer and the dreamed, the awaker and the dream, are all equal. If waking were dependent upon something else, Then perhaps the dream would not exist."

As for "waiting": when there is no waiting, one stands alone. What defiled phenomena could there be to lead or bestow? Observing awakening and dreaming through this, one sees that their opening and closing are not different.
It is only due to habitual customs and arbitrary attachments that people claim there is truth or falsehood between dreaming and awakening.
Just as dreams vanish of themselves when the eyes are closed, so too does the light of my original awakening—not confined by either waking or dreaming—illuminate all things from the very beginning.
Without entanglement, if clarity has not yet arisen, even awakening and dreams have no ground. Understanding this, one may turn the sutra;
using this wordless sutra, the wordless turns without ceasing. Throughout the dust-motes and lands, it resounds with blazing speech.
Regarding the verse on Ācārya Kumārajīva receiving the bowl:

when he was without mind, he received the bowl; the bowl had neither lightness nor heaviness. When there was the mind of discrimination, the bowl became heavy and he could not bear it. Viewed from this perspective, [the truth is clear].
Objects and self are fundamentally non-existent; they are established through conceptual discrimination. It is like when a person steps on a purple eggplant by mistake and suspects it is a toad;
with eyes closed, he seeks its life, but upon opening his eyes, he sees only the eggplant—the toad has no trace. You, as a son of the Buddha, should constantly maintain this contemplation.
The myriad dharmas are non-dharmas; the mind gives rise to them as if they were arbitrarily existent. Birth-and-death and afflictions are likewise so.

To manifest that for a layperson begging for rice, the wheel of food precedes the turning of the wheel of Dharma: sweet rain pours through the night like a spring, and when the wheat ripens, do not say it is not the Buddha's work.
Power. At Heishan Yen-ch'ing, causes and conditions are joined.
Whether it be sun or rain, they are impermanent;
before Wan-fo-tsang, one contemplates the moonlight. Within the moon there is no rain—this is the reality. As for the rain at Heishan Yen-ch'ing, what is it?

Come! May it universally moisten those far and near, bringing benefit to all. If the nature of rain and the nature of sun were constant, the Sage would feel ashamed of his virtue for not being in accord with Heaven.
One must know that the matters of cloud and sun follow conditions; where the conditioning is ripe, the power of karma exerts its force.

The verse on the "Miao-an" (Subtle Hermitage) character reveals that when compassion manifests and the sense bases and objects fall away, this mind suddenly appears. Its manifestation is subtle and wondrous; it is difficult for intellect and consciousness to perceive. In daily life, it is ever-vibrant and luminous.
Having traversed the mountains and rivers, he returned to report to his fundamental source. Only upon seeing the verse did the proof begin to manifest.
He showed the *zhitan* (pointing-fist) hand-gesture and recited this verse:
"Sentient beings burn with the fire of ignorance; clinging to the body, they produce birth and death. The Sage, pitying their folly, teaches them to contemplate the 'one-four'."
Seeing the four, one is clearly unconfused; the single body cannot be apprehended. This washes away the defilements of ordinary beings; it is not the clinging of the two vehicles.

Furthermore, by means of the one, the four are dispelled, yet the four likewise cannot be apprehended. Since both the one and the four do not exist, there is directly beneath this the wisdom of non-arising.
It cannot be sought through calculation; it cannot be met through emotion. When both emotion and calculation are completely severed, there is a mass of flesh that is the adamantine body.
It is like a hand forming a fist: some perceive the fist as the hand, while others perceive the hand as the fist.
If the fist possessed the nature of a fist, it could not be made by the hand; if the hand possessed the nature of a hand, it could not be made into a fist.

Since both the fist and the hand lack inherent nature, how can the one who grasps them not be deluded? Although they lack the nature of fist and hand, the fist and hand nonetheless appear vividly as such.
Who among those we encounter will take up this gāthā of my clenched fist? Having confidence that it accords with the Buddha-mind, the dragons and spirits shall reverently protect and uphold it.
May all who wish to see or hear it realize the principle of non-arising.
The old woman threw her child into the water;
as soon as its foul mouth opened, she struck it with a single oar. The old woman had no way to clear away the stench;
she took the infant and cast him into the cold waves, provoking a clamor among fish and dragons throughout the four seas.
The verse on the occasion of Deshan’s alms-round:
The circumstances of the alms-round are not at all difficult; a secret whispering by the ear is the profound barrier. Meeting within the inner depths, one knows the place of return;
ten thousand wonders and a thousand mysteries occur in a single moment.
Spontaneous Verse:
Falling petals fill the ground; spring is already deep. In the empty hall throughout the long day, the Sanskrit sounds are chanted.
If you wish for the spirit-mansion to be devoid of a single thing, You should carefully examine the mind through the four aggregates.
The Verse on the Poisoned Drum:

One may perceive the body as the go-between for birth and death; yet, when there is even a slight awareness, hatred and attachment arise as its very foundation. If a person realizes that both are devoid of intrinsic nature, then whether objects and conditions are favorable or adverse, they are like a drum smeared with lethal poison.
The Verse on Subduing Māra:
When a person practices with diligence, within the realms of movement and stillness, all perceptions of good and evil are manifestations of one's own mind.
Therefore, one who has attained mastery over their own mind cannot be deluded by any demons. For those who have not yet attained this mastery, those [demons] appear and act as if they were real.
Apart from one’s own mind, all phenomena cannot be found. If there were a demon within that which cannot be found, how would it differ from seeking a fierce flame within layered ice?
Thus, when one observes with discernment that the self-mind is empty, the mind being empty and objects stilled, no demon exists.
Since no demon exists, no Buddha arises; where no Buddha arises, light fills all. Those who have the karmic affinity to behold this light will follow [the path].
The pivotal point is ever sovereign; by maintaining this sovereignty, one delivers all sentient beings. The lamp of the Buddha shines eternally and exhaustlessly.
All factions of Māra should protect and uphold it; if this verse is not protected and upheld, the race of Māra cannot survive.
The Verse on the Intertwining Reeds:
All phenomena are like intertwining reeds; when one fully realizes this, what is there to prefer or loathe? Like a thirsty deer chasing a mirage, the closer it comes, the more it vanishes.

A fleeting thought of ordinary or holy gives rise to grasping and rejecting within a dream. I yield this to the Ox of Mount Mui, who sleeps contentedly in the deep green, his needs satisfied by water alone.
Inscription on the Wall of Hanshan Temple in Gusu: The likenesses of Hanshan and Shishi are like the void;
their intent is like metal and stone. Whether ancient or modern, though they face one another, they remain unrecognized.
Furthermore, its wondrous peaks are difficult to describe in terms of their skeletal structure; the drifting clouds provide no metaphor for its spirit.
I do not know whose son he was, yet how transcendent, vast, profound, and refined he was!
Furthermore:
When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and consumes empty space, these two *dhūtas* are merely blowing wind.
If you ask where they dwell, look for their traces upon the fine beard of Ke-lang.

Inscription for Mingyue Temple The void is the source of the myriad phenomena; the profound and distant is the gateway of the spirit. To shut one’s door and sever the root—upon what can one rely to advance in virtue?
Alas! In this realm of non-action, it is difficult to escape from falling away. A stagnant pool does not harbor dragons; to harbor a dragon, one requires living water.
It is like a single branch of blossoms; how could the springtime have an end? Though these words are indeed plain, their flavor possesses considerable reason.

Inscribed on a Stone Chamber in a Bamboo Grove: Where is there no green mountain? A fragment of mind cooled and extinguished is difficult; a fragment of mind cooled and extinguished is easy. With wisdom, one pulls back ten thousand layers of barriers.

The Master took up the final phrase and questioned Tanwen. Wen replied, “Where the bamboo is dense, it does not hinder the flowing stream; though the mountain is high, how could it obstruct the flying white clouds?
The Master commanded Wen to perform three prostrations and said, “First move with concentration, then extract with wisdom.
What you have said cannot avoid being an established fact.”
The Verse on the Five-Colored Excrement:
When the mindfulness of both men and women is unmoving, the red and white do not flow. Since the red and white do not flow, how can my body be obtained?
If my mindfulness is unmoving, it is difficult for the red and white to take hold. Contemplating these three conditions with discernment, the body and mind are like flames at the bottom of ice.
If there were flames at the bottom of ice, the ice would no longer be called ice. The wise contemplate in this way, entering deeply as if into samādhi.
Lying beneath a grove of a hundred flowers is no different from being in a desolate cemetery. When a sacred altar becomes a desolate cemetery, who among those who wander would remain?
Even if there were fragrant bait offered, he would not deign to eat it; terrified by the tugging of his arm, how could he dare cast even a glance back?

The Verse on Destroying Attachments:

If this pain is what is being pained, then it is one and the same. Since that oneness is fundamentally devoid of subject and object, who is it that experiences the pain?

You must directly take all the various feelings of hatred and love within this suffering, as well as the consciousness of those feelings of hatred and love, and transform them into a single act of contemplation.
Risk your life and persevere until you ultimately know who it is that feels the pain—regard this as your primary pursuit. If you truly investigate...

Once you have attained entry into the head, not only will karma be exhausted and pain eliminated, but I can venture to guarantee that the entire practice of Zen meditation shall be brought to a final conclusion from this point forward.
Therefore, there were many among the ancients who, amidst their illnesses, realized the ground of the mind.

Thus, when people of old saw that illness did not come to them, they felt shame and fear, weeping with grief as they privately and painfully reproached themselves, thinking: "This must be because the Buddhas have abandoned me and are not bestowing their secret grace upon me."
If you are willing to receive their secret empowerment, then illness will not depart. Why is this?

It is because sentient beings, since immeasurable kalpas past, have become deluded regarding the fundamentally luminous, vast, and spiritually resonant essence, as well as the lively and pure mind; they instead cling to these floating thoughts.
And yet, you cherish and cling to this foul carcass, refusing to let it go.
If you were tormented by the pain of illness, sentient beings would naturally realize that this body is precarious and fragile, foul, filthy, and impure.

When such a thought arises, if one further receives the gentle prodding and subtle striking of a virtuous friend, they will see that this body is foul and filthy, unfit for cherishing; its appearance is unreal—so why harbor hatred toward it?
Affection! This patient is truly a person of heroic spirit. Upon hearing these words, he disregards not only these physical ailments;

even if flying arrows pierce his eyes or a drawn blade strikes his chest, he has no leisure to concern himself with the foul husk of this body, for he only regrets that his contemplation is not yet matured and that he has not attained clear penetration toward the Ultimate. Such is the principle.
It is just as with Heaven: when it warns a compassionate ruler, it manifests portents such as comets. Today, while the universe is at peace, you have resolved to investigate this Great Matter;
thus, these demonic afflictions and sufferings have arisen. This is truly the secret empowerment of all Buddhas bestowed upon you.
One must not fail to reflect upon this. When I, a poor monk, observe that you suffer from such an ailment, I am both concerned for you and yet filled with joy for you.

In response to Qiu Qianqian’s three-part discourse on the unmanifested states of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure—where it is said that the state prior to their manifestation is called "the Center" (zhong)—since this Center is described as "unmanifested," who can know what is within it?

When [the mind] has been aroused, there is cognitive awareness by which one may know whether it is in the state of "central equilibrium" (*zhong*) or not yet in that state. When it has not yet been aroused, there is no thought;
where there is no thought, there is no cognitive awareness. Regarding what is commonly called the "central equilibrium of the unaroused," by what means can its centrality be perceived?

If one uses that which has already been aroused to verify the unaroused state and thereby knows its centrality, then that which has already been aroused is not identical to the unaroused state. The unaroused...

If one does not act immediately upon having aroused [the mind], then it is impossible to verify the unaroused state by means of the aroused state. Within this context, the fundamental principle of the Confucian school has remained unclear for a long time.
I pray that you, sir, being of such high intelligence, erudition, and refinement, will graciously provide an exposition of this matter.

Since it is said that [the mind] is "unmanifested," it is fundamentally without thought. Without thought, there is no cognition; yet, one is able to perceive this state of being unmanifested—is this through knowledge or not through knowledge?
If it is through knowledge, then it has already been manifested. If it is without knowledge, then who knows what is within it?
If you say it is known spontaneously, do you mean it is known by means of a self, or known without a self? If there is a self, it is not spontaneous. If there is no self, then...
Who naturally knows this? Your Highness’s response was broad and general, yet you have not seen the underlying point of my inquiry.

Generally speaking, every debate must have a central thesis; its value lies in the answer being rooted in the question and the question being rooted in the answer, like the tips of two arrowheads meeting or a box and its lid fitting perfectly. Therefore, one must not fail to contemplate and discern the very origins of the question with precision.

Regarding the establishment of this thesis: the present establishment of the thesis concerns that which has not yet been manifested. Since there is no thought or cognition therein, how can one know it as "not yet manifested"?

If one uses what has already been manifested to infer what has not yet been manifested, then one concludes that what has already been manifested is incorrect, and what has not yet been manifested is likewise incorrect;

however, such a principle does not exist. For "the state before manifestation" is vast and traceless, resembling the great void. Even if one errs regarding what has already been manifested, where could one find a place of error within that?
It is capable of being accumulated. If it were possible for that which is capable of being accumulated to be attained, then even empty space could be painted with colors.
I only ask that you, Master, examine my questions and answers with care regarding their essential purport, and instruct me in detail.
What Gao Ming calls "the essence of natural, luminous awareness" is precisely this "centrality prior to the arousal [of thought].

Does he mean that it is known as the centrality prior to arousal because luminous awareness knows itself? Or does he mean that it is known as its centrality because of the arising of thought and the subsequent act of cognitive illumination?
If one knows by oneself, then the blade does not cut itself, nor does the eye see itself. To know through the arising of a thought means it belongs to that which has already been aroused;
it cannot be called the state of the "unmoved center."

I tell you, Layman Hu Dexiu, that from antiquity until now, those who have largely failed to accomplish the Way have generally done so because they could not bring their own body and mind under control.
Consequently, birth-and-death and hatred-and-love intermingle, agitating the spiritual palace (lingtai) until it is turbid; for even a single moment, one cannot attain clarity.
Alas! You do not know at all what summons birth and death, nor how hatred and love are formed.

Though you may rush to and fro across lakes and seas, seeking the Truth and searching for secret instructions to cure your body and mind—whether those things obtained by seeing with the eyes or heard with the ears—[you remain ignorant].

They huddle their heads together to transmit [the teachings], relying on forced manipulations. Furthermore, having attained a small measure of illumination within stillness, they mistake it for the ultimate goal.
For years and throughout their days, they merely dally with the "ghost-eye" and puff out the breath of worldly sustenance; they fail to rectify their own body and mind by even a hair’s breadth.
Should they encounter times of upheaval and exile, or the fields of opposition, favor, right, and wrong, they remain as before—caught in birth and death.
Haoran, your likes and dislikes fill your breast; they flutter and sway about you, making it feel as if there were thorns piercing your very heart-mind.
This is because you do not know the source of your own body and mind. Since you do not know the source of body and mind, the obstructions of this very body and mind are no small matter.
If you continue to act in such a lackluster manner, not only will you find it difficult to fully awaken to the Great Way, but you will remain stuck in delusion.

Throughout one's daily life, I dare say that from birth until death, one has not even dreamed of finding peace and ease. Why is this? If one does not know the source of the body, one perceives the existence of a body;
because one perceives the existence of a body, one suffers the burden of the body. If one does not know the source of the mind, one perceives the existence of a mind;
because one perceives the existence of a mind, one suffers the toil of the mind. Master Sengzhao said: "There is no toil more laborious than the possession of intellect."
"There is no greater affliction than having a body. How could this deceive me? Now, speak of the source from which this body and mind arise.
This present physical shell is nothing more than a composite of the four great elements; it is clearly discernible before us.
This point of deluded mind is nothing more than a gathering of the four aggregates. Sentient beings are inverted, falsely taking this body to be a self and this mind to be... [a self].

The mind has been sinking and falling for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, without end. Changing heads and faces, it spreads like fire passing from one piece of wood to another, without ceasing.
You who are great men seeking the Way with a true heart—why not exert your full brilliance? Beat your breast and judge for yourself; give rise to a single, resolute will of determination.
At once, push away the body by means of the four elements, and push away the mind by means of the four aggregates. When encountering conditions or touching objects, [remain thus].
From early morning until evening, it continues incessantly. Joy is examined in this way; affliction is examined in this way.
Pushing and examining back and forth, one’s practice becomes mature. Suddenly, body and mind are vast and open, utterly empty and luminous.
Reaching such a state, what would De Xiu ultimately call "body and mind"? What would he call "birth and death," or "hatred and love"?
"Dexiu has indeed truly taken up the burden. What you have accomplished not only makes you a candidate for Buddhahood, but there is also a path for you to become an immortal.

The fundamental source. Even all Buddhas have not yet glimpsed it in their dreams. But tell me: what is this fundamental source that transcends?
Where are the Buddhas of the ten directions? They are all within the wombs of donkeys and horses.

The Buddha’s light is the light of the monk. When concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are both strong, concentration empties the passions while wisdom manifests the nature. These two contend with one another;
when one prevails, the other perishes. This is not a matter of mere verbal explanation, but must be realized by the mind and practiced through action.

"To set forth one's will is like lighting a lamp; 'will' is where the mind resides, and a 'lamp' is that which shines brightly to dispel darkness. Once darkness is dispelled from the ground of the mind, it naturally becomes lofty and brilliant.
When the ground of the mind is thus lofty and brilliant, great men and gentlemen will no longer look down upon you."

To drift along with Yu Zhongfu is to follow a divergent path; when emotions become a burden, if one does not sever them when it is time to do so, how can one be released from these hidden fetters? As it is said:
"Show me as if you have heard."
Sentient beings engage in arbitrary conceptualizations that shroud their original mind; therefore, amidst the functioning of the total embodiment, they harbor doubts and are unable to employ it.
One night, I bent my finger and asked Ruwen, "Do you see it? He replied, "I see it. I asked, "Can you see anything outside of this?
He replied, "I do not know. I sighed deeply for a long time and then pointed it out to him, saying, "This finger of mine—"
In a single contraction, all sages and ordinary beings, all environments and inhabitants—there is not a single dharma that can be extended.

Not only is this contraction thus, but every dharma is likewise so. It is like a single thought-moment arising and ceasing: when it arises, it arises simultaneously with the entirety of the realm of empty space.
There is not even a space the size of a mustard seed where cessation could be contained; cessation is likewise thus.
Vimalakīrti said to Maitreya, "All sentient beings are suchness. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī replied to Vimalakīrti, "Householder, I have come with the characteristic of non-coming.
Had there been an initial coming, I would not be able to see you, householder, now. From this it may be said:
It is clear that non-coming is not coming, and coming is not non-coming. Only those who thoroughly understand their own minds will gradually break through emotional views;
by attaining a single dharma within this Dharma-gate, they will realize every dharma.

"These two. I request that the Master explain them. The Master said, "The nature of the mind is originally non-dual.

is this not the clarification of the mind? When one sees the nature, the mind becomes clear of itself; it is not that one must first clarify the mind in order to be able to see the nature."
The Master said: "Master Zhigong said that while sitting or lying down, one does not know that this very state is the Way;
thus one merely rushes about in haste, undergoing bitter toil. The Master further said: "The Way is like water. In water there are fish—some as large as thousands of li, others as small as a hair.

Thus, fish, regardless of their size, are entirely identical to water. To contemplate in this manner is the principle; it is not the emotion. Emotion has no root;
it arises from the transformation of the self-nature (*svabhāva*). That which is without self yet possesses spiritual clarity is the nature; that which possesses self and is obscured is emotion.
The multitude generally act according to that which possesses self and is obscured when dealing with affairs; therefore, they are unable to penetrate the world.
The Sage follows the state of non-self, and his numinous spirit responds to affairs;

thus he is able to penetrate the sentiments of the world, such that neither good fortune nor misfortune can burden him. Although the explanation is thus, if names are not examined, their meanings will not be refined.

If the meaning is not refined, the principle will not be penetrated. If the principle is not penetrated, the nature will not be fully realized. If the nature is not fully realized, yet one wishes to reach the stage of destiny (*jìng*), there is no such possibility.
Now, destiny is function; when this function manifests before us, space can be rolled up or spread out, and existence and non-existence can be made into a single thread.
The Buddha taught that the two dharmas of existence and non-existence encompass all phenomena. Therefore, as for...
The one who commands acts before Heaven, yet Heaven does not oppose him. If even Heaven does not oppose him, how could the myriad things oppose him?
Such meanings may be spoken with smooth and flowing eloquence, and those who hear them easily give rise to joy; yet, this must be applied so that it manifests in the present moment.

The roots of feverish affliction have not been uprooted; the dream of coolness has never awakened. To say this is "exhausting one's nature" (*jinxing*) is acceptable, but to say it is "reaching the destiny of life" (*zhuyuming*) is not.
An ancient worthy said: "If one does not undergo a single instance of cold that penetrates to the very bones, how can one obtain the fragrance of plum blossoms wafting through the nose?
Now, as for "cold penetrating to the bones," it is like Yan Hui’s casting off of his physical form and discarding of his cleverness; this too is such a case.
This is a minor matter. For if the limbs and body are disintegrated, the "body" cannot be found; if one is clever and cunning, the "mind" cannot be found.

Since both body and mind are unfindable, the emotions die and the nature (xing) becomes alive. When the nature is alive, these very limbs and body are the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), and this very cleverness is Prajñā.

The manner in which [the teaching] arises is like this; the humble return to the primal truth is likewise so. When it comes to literary expression, one must seek dynamic transformation rather than being confined by rigid, dead forms.

Seven days after the Buddha was born, his mother was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. When the Buddha had left home, attained the Way, and was about to universally deliver all sentient beings, he reflected:
"My mother has not yet been delivered; should I not deliver her first before delivering other beings? Is this not placing my own mother before others?
Thereupon, he ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and preached the Dharma for his mother. Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, his mother’s mind was also opened.

One attains the Way. Judging from this, the filial piety that consists in serving one’s parents while alive and burying them after death—considering such filial piety as the duty of a son to stop at this alone—I fear it is not the universal path for all under heaven.
Speaking in terms of supreme filial piety, if a son can, like the Buddha, preach the Dharma for his mother so that she too attains the Way, only such filial piety may be called ultimate.

It is simply filial piety. Therefore it is said: "Filial piety through form is emotion (*qing*); filial piety through principle (*li*) is nature (*xing*). Emotion is characterized by the presence of self and is obscure;
nature is characterized by the absence of self and is spiritual. Where there is a self, there is no emptiness; where there is no emptiness, there is no spiritual clarity.
Where there is no self, there is emptiness and spiritual clarity. Thus, one practices filial piety with that which is neither empty nor spiritually clear.

Filial piety never fails to reach its fruition. To practice filial piety with a spirit of sincerity and spiritual resonance—yet to claim that such filial piety does not reach its goal—is impossible; it has never occurred.
Now, this layman of Wu is resolved to reverently serve the auspicious sandalwood image, desiring that his mother’s life end in hearing the Dharma, her mind opening, and her attaining the Way.
This, too, is the heart of the Buddha. Nevertheless, for the sake of sentient beings, the Buddha established filial piety as the fundamental principle (*mūla*). This is the principle.
When this is established, the world has a sovereign. Having a sovereign, the ears and eyes do not turn to two directions.

When the ears and eyes do not turn to two directions, the mind does not require deliberation to become unified of its own accord. When the mind is unified, the "self" that is obscure diminishes daily, while the "no-self" that is numinous grows daily.

If one knows that the "unified aggregate" (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*) can be broken down into "many fragmented aggregates," then the many fragmented aggregates will break the unified aggregate.

This verse consists of twenty characters in total; yet it encompasses, without exception, the four noble beings and the six classes of ordinary beings, the ten dharma-realms, and both the primary and secondary retributions.

Within the six paths of rebirth, the three miserable realms are evil mental states;
humans, asuras, and devas—these three—are good mental states; and śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas are all pure mental states.

It is not a matter of defiled emotion. Viewed from this perspective, although gods, humans, and asuras are superior to those in the three miserable realms, they are all transformations of the mind’s capacity for both the wholesome and the defiled.
Therefore it is said: "When the emotions of both ordinary beings and sages are exhausted, the essence reveals the true permanence;
this true permanence is precisely the Mind-only. Alas! As for the function of the Mind-only, it is the same whether one is a sage or a common person, a Buddha or a sentient being.

None of these have ever failed to be complete. It is simply that ordinary people and sentient beings utilize them daily without realizing it, whereas sages and Buddhas utilize them daily without being deluded.
This is the reason for the distinction between the four types of sages and the six classes of ordinary beings.

Human beings are the most spiritual among all things. If one cannot know what lies before the four sages and the six classes of ordinary beings, then one cannot act as the master over the transformations of those four sages and six classes.

It is further said: "Heaven and earth share the same root; the myriad things are one body. Therefore, when those who are alive attain enlightenment, those who have passed away find peace of mind;
